claim: Linguistic phrases are tracked in sentences even though there is no one-to-one acoustic phrase marker in the physical signal.
source: Linguistic phrases are tracked in sentences even though there is no one-to-one acoustic phrase marker in the physical signal.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that motivates the study.

claim: Phrasal tracking suggests an automatic tracking of abstract linguistic structure that is endogenously generated by the brain.
source: This phenomenon suggests an automatic tracking of abstract linguistic structure that is endogenously generated by the brain.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the phrasal tracking phenomenon in the abstract.

claim: Previous studies investigating linguistic tracking compare conditions where relevant information at linguistic timescales is available versus conditions where this information is absent.
source: However, all studies investigating linguistic tracking compare conditions where either relevant information at linguistic timescales is available, or where this information is absent altogether (e.g., sentences versus word lists during passive listening).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous research in the abstract.

claim: The study presented participants with sentences and word lists while recording brain activity with MEG.
source: To investigate this question, we presented participants with sentences and word lists while recording their brain activity with magnetoencephalography (MEG).
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Participants performed passive, syllable, word, and word-combination tasks corresponding to attending to four different rates.
source: Participants performed passive, syllable, word, and word-combination tasks corresponding to attending to four different rates: one they would naturally attend to, syllable-rates, word-rates, and phrasal-rates, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental tasks used in the study.

claim: The study replicated findings of stronger phrasal-rate tracking measured with mutual information for sentences compared to word lists across the classical language network.
source: We replicated overall findings of stronger phrasal-rate tracking measured with mutual information for sentences compared to word lists across the classical language network.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: In the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), there was a task effect suggesting stronger phrasal-rate tracking during the word-combination task independent of the presence of linguistic structure.
source: However, in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) we found a task effect suggesting stronger phrasal-rate tracking during the word-combination task independent of the presence of linguistic structure, as well as stronger delta-band connectivity during this task.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: There was stronger delta-band connectivity during the word-combination task in IFG.
source: However, in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) we found a task effect suggesting stronger phrasal-rate tracking during the word-combination task independent of the presence of linguistic structure, as well as stronger delta-band connectivity during this task.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: Extracting linguistic information at phrasal rates occurs automatically with or without the presence of an additional task.
source: These results suggest that extracting linguistic information at phrasal rates occurs automatically with or without the presence of an additional task, but also that IFG might be important for temporal integration across various perceptual domains.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results in the abstract.

claim: IFG might be important for temporal integration across various perceptual domains.
source: These results suggest that extracting linguistic information at phrasal rates occurs automatically with or without the presence of an additional task, but also that IFG might be important for temporal integration across various perceptual domains.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results in the abstract.

claim: Understanding spoken language requires a multitude of processes.
source: Understanding spoken language likely requires a multitude of processes (Friederici, 2011; Martin, 2020; Halle and Stevens, 1962).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Acoustic patterns must be segmented and mapped onto internally-stored phonetic and syllabic representations.
source: Although not always an exclusively bottom-up affair, acoustic patterns must be segmented and mapped onto internally-stored phonetic and syllabic representations (Halle and Stevens, 1962; Marslen-Wilson and Welsh, 1978; Martin, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Phonemes must be combined and mapped onto words, which in turn form abstract linguistic structures such as phrases.
source: Phonemes must be combined and mapped onto words, which in turn form abstract linguistic structures such as phrases (e.g., Martin, 2020; Pinker and Jackendoff, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: It is essential to track the temporal dynamics of the speech signal in order to understand its meaning.
source: It has been shown that it is essential to track the temporal dynamics of the speech signal in order to understand its meaning (e.g., Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Peelle and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In natural speech, syllables follow each other in the theta range (3–8 Hz).
source: In natural speech, syllables follow each other in the theta range (3–8 Hz; Rosen, 1992; Ding et al., 2017; Pellegrino et al., 2011), while higher-level linguistic features such as words and phrases tend to occur at lower rates (0.5–3 Hz; Rosen, 1992; Kaufeld et al., 2020; Keitel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Higher-level linguistic features such as words and phrases tend to occur at lower rates (0.5–3 Hz).
source: In natural speech, syllables follow each other in the theta range (3–8 Hz; Rosen, 1992; Ding et al., 2017; Pellegrino et al., 2011), while higher-level linguistic features such as words and phrases tend to occur at lower rates (0.5–3 Hz; Rosen, 1992; Kaufeld et al., 2020; Keitel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tracking of syllabic features is stronger when one understands a language.
source: Tracking of syllabic features is stronger when one understands a language (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Zoefel et al., 2018a; Doelling et al., 2014) and tracking of phrasal rates is more prominent when the signal contains phrasal information (Kaufeld et al., 2020; Keitel et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2016; e.g., word lists versus sentences).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tracking of phrasal rates is more prominent when the signal contains phrasal information.
source: Tracking of syllabic features is stronger when one understands a language (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Zoefel et al., 2018a; Doelling et al., 2014) and tracking of phrasal rates is more prominent when the signal contains phrasal information (Kaufeld et al., 2020; Keitel et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2016; e.g., word lists versus sentences).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Phrasal tracking occurs even when there are no distinct acoustic modulations at the phrasal rate.
source: Importantly, phrasal tracking even occurs when there are no distinct acoustic modulations at the phrasal rate (Kaufeld et al., 2020; Keitel et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Overall task performance was above chance and participants complied with task instructions.
source: Overall task performance was above chance and participants complied with task instructions (Figure 1; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for individual data).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1.

source: We found a significant interaction between condition and task (F(2,72.0) = 11.51, p < 0.001) as well as a main effect of task (F(2,19.7) = 44.19, p < 0.001) and condition (F(2,72.0) = 29.0, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result reported in the Results section.

claim: There was a main effect of task on behavioral performance (F(2,19.7) = 44.19, p < 0.001).
source: We found a significant interaction between condition and task (F(2,72.0) = 11.51, p < 0.001) as well as a main effect of task (F(2,19.7) = 44.19, p < 0.001) and condition (F(2,72.0) = 29.0, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result reported in the Results section.

claim: There was a main effect of condition on behavioral performance (F(2,72.0) = 29.0, p < 0.001).
source: We found a significant interaction between condition and task (F(2,72.0) = 11.51, p < 0.001) as well as a main effect of task (F(2,19.7) = 44.19, p < 0.001) and condition (F(2,72.0) = 29.0, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result reported in the Results section.

claim: Only for the word-combination (phrasal-level) task, the sentence condition had a significantly higher accuracy than the word list condition (t(54.0) = 6.97, p < 0.001).
source: We found that only for the word-combination (phrasal-level) task, the sentence condition had a significantly higher accuracy than the word list condition (t(54.0) = 6.97, p < 0.001).

claim: For the syllable task, no significant condition effect on accuracy was found (t(54.0) = 0.62, p = 1.000).

claim: For the word task, no significant condition effect on accuracy was found (t(54.0) = 1.74, p = 0.176).

claim: For the phrasal timescale in STG, there was significantly higher MI in the sentence compared to the word list condition (F(3,126) = 67.39, p < 0.001).
source: For the phrasal timescale in STG, we found significantly higher MI in the sentence compared to the word list condition (F(3,126) = 67.39, p < 0.001; Figure 3; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual data).

source: No other effects were significant (p > 0.1).

claim: The STG phrasal MI finding paralleled the effect found in Kaufeld et al., 2020.
source: This finding paralleled the effect found in Kaufeld et al., 2020.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work in the Results section.

source: For the MTG, we saw a different picture: Besides the main effect of condition (F(3,126) = 50.24, p < 0.001), an interaction between task and condition was found (F(3,126) = 2.948, p = 0.035).

claim: For the MTG phrasal MI, an interaction between task and condition was found (F(3,126) = 2.948, p = 0.035).
source: For the MTG, we saw a different picture: Besides the main effect of condition (F(3,126) = 50.24, p < 0.001), an interaction between task and condition was found (F(3,126) = 2.948, p = 0.035).

source: We next investigated the effect of condition per task and found for all tasks except the passive task a significant effect of condition, with stronger MI for the sentence condition (passive: t(126) = 1.07, p = 0.865; syllable: t(126) = 4.06, p = 0.003; word: t(126) = 5.033, p < 0.001; phrase: t(126) = 4.015, p = 0.003).

source: For the IFG, we found a main effect of condition (F(3,108) = 21.89, p < 0.001) as well as a main effect of task (F(3,108) = 2.74, p = 0.047).

claim: For the IFG phrasal MI, there was a main effect of task (F(3,108) = 2.74, p = 0.047).

source: For the word and syllable frequency bands no interactions were found (all p > 0.1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

source: For the delta band, we found for the STG a main effect of condition (F(1,18) = 6.11, p = 0.024; Figure 4. See Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for individual data) and task (F(3,108) = 3.069, p = 0.031).

source: For the delta band, we found for the STG a main effect of condition (F(1,18) = 6.11, p = 0.024; Figure 4. See Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for individual data) and task (F(3,108) = 3.069, p = 0.031).

source: Overall, the amount of PCA components did not influence any of the qualitative differences in the condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section for the number of component control.

claim: 10 PCA components were not sufficient to show all original effects with the same power.
source: It did seem however that 10 PCA components were not sufficient to show all original effects with the same power.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section for the number of component control.

claim: The IFG task and MTG task × condition effect were only trend significant for 10 components (p = 0.06 and p = 0.1, respectively).
source: Specifically, the IFG task and MTG task × condition effect were only trend significant for 10 components (p = 0.06 and p = 0.1, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section for the number of component control.

claim: Using 30 components made some effects stronger than with 20 components.
source: Using 30 components made some of our effects stronger than with 20 components.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section for the number of component control.

claim: With 30 components, the IFG task and MTG task × condition effects had p values of 0.034 and 0.006, respectively.
source: Here, the IFG task and MTG task × condition effects had p values of 0.034 and 0.006, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section for the number of component control.

claim: The amount of PCA components did not qualitatively change any of the reported effects.
source: We conclude that the amount of PCAs components did not qualitative change any of our reported effects.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section for the number of component control.

claim: Different nodes of the language network showed different tracking patterns.
source: Different nodes of the language network showed different tracking patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section.

claim: Tracking at phrasal timescales depends both on the linguistic information present in the signal, and on the specific task that is performed.
source: This suggests that tracking at phrasal timescales depends both on the linguistic information present in the signal, and on the specific task that is performed.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: The findings reported in this study are in line with previous results, with overall stronger tracking of low-frequency information in the sentences compared to the word list condition.
source: The findings reported in this study are in line with previous results, with overall stronger tracking of low-frequency information in the sentences compared to the word list condition (Kaufeld et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: For the stimuli used in this study, it has been shown that the condition effects are not due to acoustic differences in the stimuli and also do not occur for reversed speech.
source: Crucially, for the stimuli used in our study it has been shown that the condition effects are not due to acoustic differences in the stimuli and also do not occur for reversed speech (Kaufeld et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: The results most likely reflect an automatic inference-based extraction of relevant phrase-level information in sentences, indicating automatic processing in participants as they understand the meaning of the speech they hear using stored, structural linguistic knowledge.
source: It is therefore most likely that our results reflect an automatic inference-based extraction of relevant phrase-level information in sentences, indicating automatic processing in participants as they understand the meaning of the speech they hear using stored, structural linguistic knowledge (Martin, 2020; Ding et al., 2016; Har-Shai Yahav and Zion Golumbic, 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Making participants pay attention to the temporal dynamics at the same hierarchical level through an additional task could not counter the main effect of condition.
source: Overall, it did not seem that making participants pay attention to the temporal dynamics at the same hierarchical level through an additional task – instructing them to remember word combinations at the phrasal rate during word list presentation – could counter this main effect of condition.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: In the MTG, increased phrasal-level tracking for sentences only occurred when participants were specifically instructed to perform an active task on the materials.
source: In the MTG we found an interaction between task and condition. In the MTG increased phrasal-level tracking for sentences only occurred when participants were specifically instructed to perform an active task on the materials.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: In MTG, all levels of linguistic information are used to do an active language operation on the stimuli.
source: It therefore seems that in MTG all levels of linguistic information are used to do an active language operation on the stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The tracking at the phrasal rate in MTG seemed relevant for behavioural performance when attending to phrasal timescales.
source: Importantly, the tracking at the phrasal rate in MTG seemed relevant for behavioural performance when attending to phrasal timescales (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section and supported by Figure 7A.

claim: Predictions flow from the highest hierarchical levels (e.g., syntax) down to lower levels (e.g., phonemes) to aid language understanding.
source: This is in line with previous theoretical and empirical research suggesting a strong top-down modulatory response of speech processing in which predictions flow from the highest hierarchical levels (e.g., syntax) down to lower levels (e.g., phonemes) to aid language understanding (Martin, 2016; Hagoort, 2017; Federmeier, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: In the word list condition, no linguistic information is present at the phrasal rate, so this information cannot be used to provide useful feedback for processing lower-level linguistic information.
source: As in the word list condition no linguistic information is present at the phrasal rate, this information cannot be used to provide useful feedback for processing lower-level linguistic information.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: MTG–STG connections were, independent of task, related to accuracy.
source: Specifically, MTG–STG connections were, independent of task, related to accuracy.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: There was higher connectivity between MTG and STG for sentences compared to word lists at low accuracies.
source: There was higher connectivity between MTG and STG for sentences compared to word lists at low accuracies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: At high accuracies, there was stronger MTG tracking at phrasal rates (measured with MI) for sentences compared to word lists during the word-combination task.
source: At high accuracies, we found that stronger MTG tracking at phrasal rates (measured with MI) for sentences compared to word lists during the word-combination task.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Tracking of phrasal structure in MTG is relevant to understand sentences compared to word lists.
source: These results suggest that indeed tracking of phrasal structure in MTG is relevant to understand sentences compared to word lists.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Participants might compensate for task difficulty using phrasal structure present in the sentence condition.
source: Participants might compensate for the difficulty using phrasal structure present in the sentence condition.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: When phrasal structure in sentences are accurately tracked (as measured with MI) performance is better when these rates are relevant.
source: When phrasal structure in sentences are accurately tracked (as measured with MI) performance is better when these rates are relevant (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section and supported by Figure 7A.

claim: Temporal tracking does not explain everything in language processing.
source: Plainly, temporal tracking does not explain everything in language processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Besides tracking there are many other components important for the designated tasks, such as memory load and semantic context which are not captured by the current analyses.
source: Besides tracking there are many other components important for our designated tasks, such as memory load and semantic context which are not captured by our current analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Both MTG and STG are strong hubs for language processing and have been involved in many studies which contrasted pseudo-words and words.
source: Both MTG and STG are strong hubs for language processing and have been involved in many studies which contrasted pseudo-words and words (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Turken and Dronkers, 2011; Vouloumanos et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: STG does the more lower-level processing of the two regions (STG and MTG), as it is earlier in the cortical hierarchy, thereby being more involved in initial segmentation and initial phonetic abstraction rather than a lexical interface.
source: It is likely that STG does the more lower-level processing of the two regions, as it is earlier in the cortical hierarchy, thereby being more involved in initial segmentation and initial phonetic abstraction rather than a lexical interface (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: STG could be earlier in a workload bottleneck, receiving feedback independent of task, while MTG feedback is recruited only when active linguistic operations are required.
source: STG could be earlier in a workload bottleneck, receiving feedback independent of task, while MTG feedback is recruited only when active linguistic operations are required.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: It is possible that small differences in the acoustics are detected by STG.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that either small differences in the acoustics are detected by STG (even though this effect was not previously found with the same stimuli, Kaufeld et al., 2020), or that our blocked designed put participants in a sentence or word list 'mode' which could have influenced the state of these early hierarchical regions.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: The blocked design might have put participants in a sentence or word list 'mode' which could have influenced the state of early hierarchical regions.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that either small differences in the acoustics are detected by STG (even though this effect was not previously found with the same stimuli, Kaufeld et al., 2020), or that our blocked designed put participants in a sentence or word list 'mode' which could have influenced the state of these early hierarchical regions.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: The IFG was the only region that showed an increase in phrasal-rate tracking specifically for the word-combination task.
source: The IFG was the only region that showed an increase in phrasal-rate tracking specifically for the word-combination task.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The comparison between the phrase task and the syllable and passive tasks only reached a trend towards significance.
source: Note, however, that this was a weak effect, as the comparison between the phrase task and the syllable and passive tasks only reached a trend towards significance.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Traditionally, IFG has been viewed as a hub for articulatory processing.
source: Traditionally, IFG has been viewed as a hub for articulatory processing (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007), but its role during speech comprehension, specifically in syntactic processing, has also been acknowledged (Friederici, 2011; Hagoort, 2017; Nelson et al., 2017; Dehaene et al., 2015; Zaccarella et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: IFG's role during speech comprehension, specifically in syntactic processing, has been acknowledged.
source: Traditionally, IFG has been viewed as a hub for articulatory processing (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007), but its role during speech comprehension, specifically in syntactic processing, has also been acknowledged (Friederici, 2011; Hagoort, 2017; Nelson et al., 2017; Dehaene et al., 2015; Zaccarella et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Integrating information across time and relative timing is essential for syntactic processing.
source: Integrating information across time and relative timing is essential for syntactic processing (Martin, 2020; Dehaene et al., 2015; Martin and Doumas, 2019), and IFG feedback has been shown to occur in temporal dynamics at lower (delta) rates during sentence processing (Park et al., 2015; Keitel and Gross, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: IFG feedback has been shown to occur in temporal dynamics at lower (delta) rates during sentence processing.
source: Integrating information across time and relative timing is essential for syntactic processing (Martin, 2020; Dehaene et al., 2015; Martin and Doumas, 2019), and IFG feedback has been shown to occur in temporal dynamics at lower (delta) rates during sentence processing (Park et al., 2015; Keitel and Gross, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Syntactic-independent verbal working memory chunking tasks recruit the IFG.
source: However, it has also been shown that syntactic-independent verbal working memory chunking tasks recruit the IFG (Dehaene et al., 2015; Osaka et al., 2004; Fegen et al., 2015; Koelsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: IFG is involved when we need to integrate across temporal domains either in a language-specific domain (sentences versus word lists) or for language-unspecific tasks (word-combination versus other tasks).
source: This is in line with our findings that show that IFG is involved when we need to integrate across temporal domains either in a language-specific domain (sentences versus word lists) or for language-unspecific tasks (word-combination versus other tasks).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The study shows increased delta connectivity with STG for the only temporal-integration tasks (i.e., the word-combination task), independent of the linguistic features in the signal.
source: We also show increased delta connectivity with STG for the only temporal-integration tasks in our study (i.e., the word-combination task), independent of the linguistic features in the signal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The results support a role of the IFG as a combinatorial hub integrating information across time.
source: Our results therefore support a role of the IFG as a combinatorial hub integrating information across time (Gelfand and Bookheimer, 2003; Schapiro et al., 2013; Skipper, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Generally, there was stronger power in the sentence condition compared to the word list condition in the delta band.
source: Generally, it seemed that there was stronger power in the sentence condition compared to the word list condition in the delta band.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The power pattern was very different than the MI pattern.
source: However, the pattern was very different than the MI pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: For the power, the word list-sentence difference was the biggest in the passive condition.
source: For the power, the word list-sentence difference was the biggest in the passive condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: For the MI, there was either no task difference (in STG) or even a stronger effect for the active tasks (in MTG).
source: In contrast, for the MI there was either no task difference (in STG) or even a stronger effect for the active tasks (in MTG; note that the power interaction was trend significant STG and MTG).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: It is unlikely that the MI effects were purely driven by SNR differences.
source: We therefore think it unlikely that our MI effects were purely driven by SNR differences, and our power control analysis is consistent with this interpretation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Power seems to reflect a different computation than the tracking, where more complex tasks generally lead to lower power across almost all tested frequency bands.
source: Instead, power seems to reflect a different computation than the tracking, where more complex tasks generally lead to lower power across almost all tested frequency bands.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Lower power did not reduce the connectivity for the delta band between IFG and STG, but rather increased it.
source: It is interesting to observe that this did not reduce the connectivity for the delta band between IFG and STG, but rather increased it.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Low power can potentially increase the available computational space, as it increases the entropy in the signal.
source: It has been suggested that low power can potentially increase the available computational space, as it increases the entropy in the signal (Hanslmayr et al., 2012; ten Oever and Sack, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Even though increased connectivity was found, there was no clear power peak in the delta band.
source: Note that even though we found increased connectivity, we did not see a clear power peak in the delta band.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The study might not be looking at an endogenous oscillator, but rather at connections operating at that temporal scale (potentially being non-oscillatory in nature).
source: This suggests that we might not be looking at an endogenous oscillator, but rather at connections operation at that temporal scale (potentially being non-oscillatory in nature).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: In the power comparisons for the theta, alpha, and beta bands, there was stronger power for the sentence compared to the word list condition, which could reflect that listening to a natural sentence is generally less effortful than listening to a word list.
source: Finally, in the power comparisons for the theta, alpha, and beta bands we found stronger power for the sentence compared to the word list condition, which could reflect that listening to a natural sentence is generally less effortful than listening to a word list.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The neural origin of the tracking of ongoing temporal dynamics is unknown.
source: In the current manuscript, we describe tracking of ongoing temporal dynamics. However, the neural origin of this tracking is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Modulations in the phrasal-rate follow changes in the phrasal rate of the acoustic input.
source: While we can be sure that modulations in the phrasal-rate follow changes in the phrasal rate of the acoustic input, it is unclear what the mechanism behind this modulation is.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: It is possible that there is stronger alignment of neural oscillations with the acoustic input at the phrasal rate.
source: It is possible that there is stronger alignment of neural oscillations with the acoustic input at the phrasal rate (Lakatos et al., 2008; Obleser and Kayser, 2019; Rimmele et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: It could be that there is a phrasal timescale or slower operation happening while processing the incoming input.
source: However, it could as well be that there is a phrasal timescale or slower operation happening while processing the incoming input (which de facto is at the same timescale as the phrasal structure inferred from the input).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: An operation in response to stimulus input could induce the patterns observed.
source: This operation, in response to stimulus input, could just as well induce the patterns we observe (Meyer et al., 2019; Zoefel et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: It is possible that there are specific responses as a consequence of the syntactic structure, task, or statistical regularities occurring as specific events at phrasal timescales.
source: Finally, it is possible that there are specific responses as a consequence of the syntactic structure, task, or statistical regularities occurring as specific events at phrasal timescales (Obleser and Kayser, 2019; Ten Oever and Martin, 2021; Frank and Yang, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: During passive listening, we naturally attend to all levels of linguistic hierarchy.
source: Our study (and many before us) indicates that during passive listening, we naturally attend to all levels of linguistic hierarchy.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The meaning of a natural sentence requires composing words in a grammatical structure.
source: This is consistent with the widely accepted notion that the meaning of a natural sentence requires composing words in a grammatical structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: For most research questions in language, it is sensible to use a task that mimics the automatic natural understanding of a sentence.
source: For most research questions in language, it therefore is sensible to use a task that mimics this automatic natural understanding of a sentence.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation in the Discussion section.

claim: Automatic understanding of linguistic information, and all the processing that this entails, cannot be countered to substantially change the consequences for neural readout, even when explicitly instructing participants to pay attention to particular timescales.
source: Here, we show that automatic understanding of linguistic information, and all the processing that this entails, cannot be countered to substantially change the consequences for neural readout, even when explicitly instructing participants to pay attention to particular timescales.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: In total, 20 Dutch native speakers (16 females; age range: 18–59; mean age = 39.5) participated in the study.
source: In total, 20 Dutch native speakers (16 females; age range: 18–59; mean age = 39.5) participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All participants were right handed, reported normal hearing, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and did not have any history of dyslexia or other language-related disorders.
source: All were right handed, reported normal hearing, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and did not have any history of dyslexia or other language-related disorders.
evidence: This describes the participant characteristics in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethical Commission for human research Arnhem/Nijmegen (project number CMO2014/288).
source: The study was approved by the Ethical Commission for human research Arnhem/Nijmegen (project number CMO2014/288).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval in the Materials and methods section.

claim: One participant was excluded from the analysis as they did not finish the full session.
source: One participant was excluded from the analysis as they did not finish the full session.
evidence: This describes participant exclusion in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Materials were identical to the stimuli used in Kaufeld et al., 2020.
source: Materials were identical to the stimuli used in Kaufeld et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the materials used in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The stimuli consisted of naturally spoken sentences or word lists which consisted of 10 words.
source: They consisted of naturally spoken sentences or word lists which consisted of 10 words (see Table 1 for examples).
evidence: This describes the stimuli in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The sentences contained two coordinate clauses with the following structure: [Adj N V N Conj Det Adj N V N].
source: The sentences contained two coordinate clauses with the following structure: [Adj N V N Conj Det Adj N V N].
evidence: This describes the sentence structure in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All words were disyllabic except for the words 'de' (the) and 'en' (and).
source: All words were disyllabic except for the words 'de' (the) and 'en' (and).
evidence: This describes the word characteristics in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Word lists were word-scrambled versions of the original sentences which always followed the structure [V V Adj Adj Det Conj N N N N] or [N N N N Det Conj V V Adj Adj] to ensure that they were grammatically incorrect.
source: Word lists were word-scrambled versions of the original sentences which always followed the structure [V V Adj Adj Det Conj N N N N] or [N N N N Det Conj V V Adj Adj] to ensure that they were grammatically incorrect.
evidence: This describes the word list structure in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In total, 60 sentences were used.
source: In total, 60 sentences were used.
evidence: This describes the number of stimuli in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The three active tasks required participants to focus on the syllabic (syllable task), word (word task), or phrasal (word combination or also called phrasal task) timescales.
source: The three active tasks required participants to focus on the syllabic (syllable task), word (word task), or phrasal (word combination or also called phrasal task) timescales.
evidence: This describes the task design in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Different trials within a task were not matched for task difficulty.
source: Note that different trials within a task were not matched for task difficulty.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the task design in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In the syllable task, syllables that make a word are much easier to recognize than syllables that do not make a word.
source: For example, in the syllable task syllables that make a word are much easier to recognize than syllables that do not make a word.
evidence: This describes task difficulty variation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Trials pertaining to the beginning of the sentence are more difficult than ones related to the end of the sentence due to recency effects.
source: Additionally, trials pertaining to the beginning of the sentence are more difficult than ones related to the end of the sentence due to recency effects.
evidence: This describes task difficulty variation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In total, there were eight blocks (two conditions × four tasks) each lasting about 8 min.
source: In total, there were eight blocks (two conditions × four tasks) each lasting about 8 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental design in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The order of the blocks was pseudo-randomized by independently randomizing the order of the tasks and the conditions.
source: The order of the blocks was pseudo-randomized by independently randomizing the order of the tasks and the conditions.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For a single participant, the same task was always presented twice in a row to avoid task-switching costs.
source: For a single participant, we then always presented the same task twice in a row to avoid task-switching costs.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in the Materials and methods section.

claim: As a consequence of presenting the same task twice in a row, condition was always alternated.
source: As a consequence, condition was always alternated (a possible order of blocks would be: passive-sentence, passive-word list, word-sentence, word-word list, syllable-sentence, syllable-word list, word-combination-sentence, word-combination-word list).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Across participants the starting condition was counterbalanced.
source: Across participants the starting condition was counterbalanced.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in the Materials and methods section.

claim: MEG was recorded using a 275-channel axial gradiometer CTF MEG system at a sampling rate of 1.2 kHz.
source: MEG was recorded using a 275-channel axial gradiometer CTF MEG system at a sampling rate of 1.2 kHz.
evidence: This describes the MEG recording parameters in the Materials and methods section.

claim: After every block participants had a break, during which head position was corrected.
source: After every block participants had a break, during which head position was corrected (Stolk et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure in the Materials and methods section.
